newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong seen spending lightly as handover looms.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong seen spending lightly as handover looms.

text.p: Hong Kong's 1997/98 spending estimates, unveiled on Thursday, showed government expenditure would remain prudent despite a handsome HK$60 billion windfall from a booming property market in the previous fiscal year.

"There is a common misunderstanding that if we get more in revenue, we can spend more," Secretary for the Treasury, K.C. Kwong said. "That is not how we control expenditure formulation in our budget."
Financial Secretary Donald Tsang is due to present the full government budget for 1997/98 on March 12.
The record land revenues are likely to boost the fiscal surplus for 1996/97 (April-March). They compare with HK$45.48 billion in the previous fiscal year.
"The main reason for the much higher revised (land earnings) estimate in 1996/97 is the buoyancy of the property market," said Kwong.
Some experts expect a fiscal surplus of HK$25 billion in the coming financial year, prompting speculation of tax cuts in a territory with a maximum personal income tax rate of 15 percent.
But Kwong said that despite the property cash crop, spending would rise only 5.3 percent to HK$248.38 billion in 1997/98.

Kwong denied that China was responsible for applying the spending brakes in the year that Hong Kong will revert to Chinese soverignty. More than 150 years of British rule of the territory ends at midnight on June 30.
"You would be bored if I say we have approached the preparation of this budget in a pragmatic, positive and cooperative manner, but that is true," said Kwong.
He stressed that Hong Kong would remain cautious in this year of great change, with spending kept below the long-term economic growth rate to comply with government policy.
Public spending would reach 18.3 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) of HK$1,355.49 billion in the coming year, well below the government limit of 20 percent of GDP, he said.
Government expenditure would rise 5.6 percent to HK$202.23 billion, with hefty boosts to education, health, social welfare and environment spending.

Kwong said government departments were responsible for the budget details and gave no hint of how the bumper land revenues would affect either the budget surplus or fiscal reserves -- among the only budget details not yet released publicly.
But estimates for property revenues next year were another sign of Hong Kong's caution. The estimate of HK$34.48 billion is well below the previous two fiscal years.

"Land revenue...depends very much on the size, location, property market situation," Kwong said. "Even if you are selling about the same amount of land in a year compared to the year before, you might get very different premia."
China was intimately involved in drawing up the budget, even though it has said it will allow Hong Kong to rule its own economic affairs for 50 years after the handover.
That is mandated in the Basic Law, the mini-constitution promulgated by China to cover Hong Kong after July 1.
Agreement on the budget was reached only days ago following 19 rounds of talks marked in the early stages by Chinese complaints that Hong Kong spending was speeding out of control.

"It's like a Formula One car which is going to crash and kill all six million people in Hong Kong," said Chen Zuo'er, leader of the mainland's budget team and a member of the Sino-British Joint Liaison Group, the diplomatic body working out the details of the transition.
Governor Chris Patten replied at the time that Hong Kong people were among the best drivers in the world.
